result:
Five versus ten is the wrong question, because "more agents always give better results" isn't true. It's a tempting idea since a bigger team of people often does more. But agents aren't people. Each one is a separate run of the loop you already know, so each one adds cost and adds chances to lose information.

Here is why that matters for your assistant:

- **Every agent has its own context.** Each one is sent its own instructions and tool descriptions, and it re-reads whatever it's handed. Tokens are what you pay for, so ten agents mean ten sets of that overhead on every request.
- **Handoffs lose detail.** When agent A passes work to agent B, B only sees what A chose to write down. It's like a function that takes a summary string instead of the real object.
- **More agents mean more places to fail.** More agents means more routing decisions, and any one of them can go wrong.

Take a real request: "Is the laser cutter free Thursday, and can I use it with acrylic?" One agent with two tools (manual search and calendar) handles that fine. Splitting it into a manual agent, a calendar agent, a safety agent and a router would make it slower and more expensive, with no gain in answer quality.

Splitting pays off in narrower cases:

- The work can run in parallel.
- One job's context would be too big to share.
- Jobs need very different tools or rules.

Start with one agent, or a fixed workflow where the steps are predictable. Add a second agent only when you can name which of those reasons applies. That's also a strong answer at your design review.

Your assistant does three jobs: answering from manuals, checking the calendar and booking. Which of those, if any, would you test first as a separate agent, and which reason from the list would justify it?
